summaryEn: The company that makes the rails AI servers slide in and out on — and earns a 78% gross margin doing it. Asia's largest server-rail maker with roughly 30% of the global market, nearly debt-free, and growing revenue more than 200% year-on-year as AI racks proliferate.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; precision-components framing — the ~30% global share, 77.7% gross margin, near-debt-free balance sheet and explosive AI-driven revenue acceleration credited, but the ~25x book valuation, single-product concentration and an UNEXPLAINED 2025Q2 one-off below the operating line flagged honestly with no cause asserted; sector/nameZh/years fixed)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
King Slide Works (川湖科技, TWSE: 2059) makes something almost nobody thinks about: **the rails that servers slide in and out of a rack on**, plus the hinges and precision mechanical components that go with them. It is the first **precision mechanical components** company in this collection — and the most improbable margin story in it. Founded on **22 September 1986** and **listed in June 2008**, it is **Asia's largest server-rail maker with roughly 30% of the global market**, and its products account for the bulk of revenue: **guide rails 70.28%**, hinges 8.42%, slides 6.95%.

The economics are extraordinary for a metal-bending business. **Gross margin is 77.74%**, operating margin **67.06%** and net margin **63.96%** — figures normally associated with software, not stamped and machined steel. Return on equity is **34.3%** on a balance sheet that is **nearly debt-free** (a **20.2% debt ratio**) and holds **NT$27.2bn of cash against NT$39.5bn of total assets**. Earnings have compounded hard: **NT$42.56 (FY2022) → 28.38 (FY2023) → 64.59 (FY2024) → NT$103.23 (FY2025)**, with dividends rising from NT$5.0 (2017) to **NT$32.2 (2024)**.

And the AI buildout has just made it violent. Revenue grew **37.8% year-on-year in 2026Q1**, then accelerated through the second quarter: **+79% in April, +172% in May, +220% in June**. AI racks are denser, heavier and serviced more often than conventional servers, and the rail systems that carry them are correspondingly more demanding — which is exactly where King Slide's share and pricing sit.

Two honest qualifications. At **NT$7,450 the stock trades on roughly 73× earnings and 25× book** with a **0.62% yield** — the market has fully recognised the story. And there is an **unexplained anomaly** in the record: in **2025Q2, net margin collapsed to 14.5% against an operating margin of 70.1%** (EPS of NT$6.45 versus NT$26.35 the prior quarter), indicating a large one-off item below the operating line for which **no published explanation could be verified**. The honest read: **a genuine, near-unassailable niche champion with software-like margins riding the AI rack boom — priced accordingly, and with one quarter in its recent history that investors should ask about.**

King Slide was founded in **1986** in Kaohsiung as a maker of **precision slides and hinges** — the mechanisms that let drawers open smoothly, cabinets close softly and panels swing without sagging. It is difficult to imagine a less glamorous starting point, and for years the company was exactly what it appeared to be: a competent Taiwanese precision-metal manufacturer. It **listed in June 2008**.

What transformed it was the **datacentre**. As computing consolidated into racks, every server needed a **rail system**: a pair of precision-engineered runners allowing a heavy machine to be pulled out for servicing while still connected, then pushed back, thousands of times, without misalignment, sag or failure. This sounds trivial and is not. A rail that binds under load, sags over years, or fails during maintenance in a facility with tens of thousands of servers is an operational disaster — so the specification is exacting, qualification is slow, and once a server maker designs a rail in, **it does not change supplier casually**.

King Slide became the company that solves this best. It built roughly **30% of the global server-rail market and the number-one position in Asia**, supplying the ODMs and brands that build the world's servers. The moat is the unglamorous kind: **decades of tooling, tolerances, testing data and design-in relationships** that a new entrant cannot buy — and which allow a maker of metal rails to charge a **77.7% gross margin**.

**AI has raised the stakes again.** AI racks are heavier, denser, hotter and often liquid-cooled, and their contents are serviced under far greater scrutiny. Rails for these systems are more demanding to engineer and command better pricing — which is why a company founded to make drawer slides is now growing revenue **more than 200% year-on-year**.

- **1986 (22 Sep)** — King Slide founded in Kaohsiung, making precision slides and hinges.
- **1990s–2000s** — Moves from furniture and industrial hardware into **server rail systems** as rack-mounted computing standardises.
- **2008 (25 Jun)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2059)**.
- **2010s** — Becomes **Asia's largest server-rail maker with roughly 30% global share**; gross margins climb toward 70%+ on design-in relationships with server ODMs and brands.
- **2022** — EPS **NT$42.56**; dividend **NT$20.0**.
- **2023** — A digestion year: EPS falls to **NT$28.38**; dividend NT$14.19.
- **2024** — AI racks lift demand: EPS **NT$64.59**; dividend **NT$32.2**.
- **2025** — **EPS NT$103.23**; gross margin around 76–78%. *(An unexplained one-off in Q2 cut that quarter's EPS to NT$6.45 despite a 70.1% operating margin.)*
- **2026** — Revenue accelerates violently: **+37.8% in Q1**, then **+79% (April), +172% (May), +220% (June)** year-on-year; 2026Q1 EPS **NT$36.58**, gross margin **77.74%**.

King Slide's financial statements are, on their face, barely believable for a mechanical-components maker.

- **Software-like margins on metal.** **Gross margin 77.74%**, **operating margin 67.06%**, **net margin 63.96%**. These are not typographical errors: they reflect a component that is **critical, specified into designs, hard to qualify and cheap relative to the server it carries** — a combination that gives extraordinary pricing power on a physically simple product.
- **A fortress balance sheet.** **Debt ratio just 20.2%**, with **NT$27.2bn of cash** out of **NT$39.5bn of total assets** and **NT$31.5bn of equity**. The company is effectively debt-free and holds cash worth well over two-thirds of its assets. **Return on equity is 34.3%** *despite* that cash drag — the operating business earns far more.
- **Compounding earnings.** Annual EPS: **NT$42.56 (FY2022) → 28.38 (FY2023) → 64.59 (FY2024) → NT$103.23 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$36.58**. Dividends followed: **NT$5.0 (2017) → 20.0 (2022) → 14.19 (2023) → NT$32.2 (2024)**.
- **An anomaly that deserves an answer.** In **2025Q2 the net margin was 14.5% while the operating margin was 70.1%**, and quarterly EPS fell to **NT$6.45 from NT$26.35**. Arithmetically this means a **large one-off charge below the operating line**. **No published explanation could be verified**, so none is asserted here — but investors should treat the **operating margin as the reliable measure** of this business and seek the cause of that quarter directly from company filings.
- **A valuation that reflects all of it.** At **NT$7,450**, roughly **73× earnings and 25× book**, yielding **0.62%**.

The financing reality: **an exceptionally profitable, cash-rich, debt-free niche monopolist** — whose accounts contain one quarter that does not fit the pattern.

**Stance: a near-unassailable niche champion earning software margins on server rails, with AI accelerating demand violently — priced at 25× book, which assumes the position and the margin both hold.**

The bull case:

1. **A genuine, quiet monopoly.** **Asia's largest server-rail maker with ~30% global share**, protected by decades of tooling, tolerances, qualification data and design-in relationships. Rails are a **tiny fraction of a server's cost but a total operational liability if they fail** — which is precisely why customers pay and do not switch.
2. **Extraordinary economics.** **77.74% gross margin, 67.06% operating margin, 34.3% ROE**, a **20.2% debt ratio** and **NT$27.2bn of cash**. Very few manufacturers anywhere earn this.
3. **AI is a step-change, not a cycle bump.** AI racks are heavier, denser and liquid-cooled, requiring more demanding rail systems at better prices. Revenue growth went from **+37.8% (Q1) to +220% (June)** — an acceleration that reflects rack deployment, not restocking.

The counter-arguments:

- **The price already assumes success.** **~73× earnings and ~25× book** with a **0.62% yield**. Even a modest deceleration would be expensive.
- **Extreme product concentration.** Guide rails and related components are **essentially the whole company**. There is no second business to cushion a design loss, a customer shift, or a change in rack architecture.
- **Margins this high invite attack.** A 78% gross margin on a mechanical component is a standing invitation to competitors and to customers' own cost-reduction programmes; the defence is qualification difficulty, not patent protection.
- **An unexplained quarter.** **2025Q2's collapse in net margin (14.5% versus a 70.1% operating margin)** has no verified cause — an outstanding question in an otherwise pristine record.

A **quality-monopoly-at-a-high-price** thesis: an outstanding business whose valuation leaves the burden of proof with continued execution.

King Slide makes money by **being designed into other people's products and then being impossible to remove cheaply**:

- **Server rail systems (the core, with guide rails alone at 70.28% of revenue).** Precision runners that allow a rack-mounted server to be extended for servicing and retracted, repeatedly, under load, without sag or misalignment. They are engineered to the specific server, tested to destruction, and **qualified into the design** by the ODM or brand. Once that happens, changing supplier means re-engineering and re-qualifying — expensive and risky for a part that is a small fraction of total system cost.
- **Hinges and precision components (8.42%)**, plus slides (6.95%) and materials — adjacent mechanical products using the same tooling and metallurgy expertise.
- **Why the margin is 78%.** Three things compound. The part is **critical** (failure is an operational disaster in a datacentre). It is **cheap relative to what it carries** (a rail costs a tiny fraction of the server, so customers optimise for reliability over price). And it is **hard to qualify** (tolerances, load ratings, cycle testing, design-in). That combination — critical, cheap, hard to replace — is one of the most reliable margin structures in manufacturing.
- **AI changes the mix upward.** AI racks are heavier, denser and increasingly liquid-cooled, demanding stronger, more precise rail systems — a **higher-specification, higher-priced product** on the same manufacturing base, which is why revenue is growing far faster than unit volumes alone would imply.

The levers are **AI rack deployment volumes, design wins at server ODMs and brands, product specification (higher-load AI rails), and manufacturing yield**. The strength is a **structural design-in moat on a critical component**. The vulnerability is that the entire company rests on **one product family sold to a concentrated set of server makers** — and the same 78% margin that proves the moat is also the reason someone will keep trying to break it.

Server mechanical components are a small, unglamorous industry sitting inside a very large one — and that positioning is the whole point.

- **A tiny cost, an enormous consequence.** Rails are a negligible fraction of a server's bill of materials, but a rail failure in a datacentre means dropped hardware, injured technicians and downtime. Buyers therefore optimise for **reliability and qualification history rather than price** — which is why a component maker can hold a 78% gross margin while its customers (server ODMs like Wiwynn and Quanta, also in this collection) operate on single-digit margins.
- **Qualification is the barrier.** Rails must be **engineered per chassis, load-tested, cycle-tested and validated** before a server ships. That process takes time and creates switching costs; the incumbent supplier is re-selected by default unless it fails. King Slide's **~30% global share and Asian leadership** rest on being that default across many designs.
- **AI raised the specification.** Rack densities, weights and liquid cooling have made mechanical requirements materially harder — favouring the supplier with the deepest engineering base and pushing the product mix toward higher-value rails.
- **Competition exists but struggles to displace.** Other Taiwanese and Chinese mechanical makers compete, and large customers periodically pursue second sources or cost-downs. The constraint is not manufacturing capability but **qualification and risk**: no datacentre operator wants to be the one that discovered a cheaper rail fails in year three.

King Slide's position is **exceptionally strong within a narrow niche**. The industry truth is that **the best margins in a supply chain often sit in its least glamorous corner** — where the part is critical, the cost is trivial and the qualification is hard. That is precisely where King Slide sits, and why an AI boom that gives server assemblers 7% gross margins gives their rail supplier 78%.

**Strengths**
- **Asia's #1 server-rail maker with ~30% global share**, protected by design-in qualification and decades of engineering data.
- **Extraordinary economics**: 77.74% gross, 67.06% operating margin, **34.3% ROE**, **20.2% debt ratio**, **NT$27.2bn cash**.
- **Violent AI-driven growth**: revenue +37.8% (Q1 2026) accelerating to **+220% year-on-year in June**; EPS **NT$42.56 → 103.23** since FY2022.

**Weaknesses**
- **Extreme product concentration** — guide rails and related components are essentially the entire business.
- **Very high valuation**: ~73× earnings, **~25× book**, 0.62% yield.
- **An unexplained 2025Q2 one-off** (net margin 14.5% versus 70.1% operating) left unresolved in the public record.

**Opportunities**
- **AI rack deployment** demanding heavier, liquid-cooled, higher-specification rail systems at better prices.
- Content growth per rack; adjacent mechanical components for AI infrastructure.
- Cash-rich balance sheet available for capacity or adjacent expansion.

**Threats**
- **Customer cost-reduction programmes** and second-sourcing aimed at a 78% gross margin.
- Rack architecture changes reducing rail content.
- Concentration among a small number of server ODMs and brands.

- **Valuation leaves no room (the immediate risk).** At **~73× earnings and ~25× book** with a **0.62% yield**, the market has priced continued hypergrowth and sustained 78% margins. The current revenue acceleration (**+220% in June**) is unlikely to persist at that rate, and the multiple assumes an orderly transition to a lower but still exceptional growth rate.
- **Single-product concentration.** Guide rails and closely related components constitute essentially all revenue. A change in rack architecture, a lost design at a major ODM, or a successful second-source qualification would hit the whole company at once.
- **Margins invite attack.** A **78% gross margin** on a mechanical part is a permanent incentive for customers to fund alternatives. The defence is qualification difficulty and risk aversion — real, but not a patent.
- **Customer concentration and cyclicality.** Demand comes from a handful of server ODMs and brands, whose orders track **hyperscaler capital spending** — the same cycle that drives Wiwynn and Quanta in this collection, and which can pause.
- **The unexplained 2025Q2 charge.** Net margin of **14.5% against a 70.1% operating margin** implies a substantial one-off below the operating line. No verified explanation exists publicly; until investors understand it, it is an open question about either the balance sheet or non-operating exposures.
- **Cash allocation.** **NT$27.2bn of cash** on a NT$39.5bn balance sheet earns little; deploying it well — or returning it — is an unresolved capital-allocation question.

King Slide's outlook is unusually simple to state and difficult to price: **it sells a critical component into the AI rack buildout at margins almost no manufacturer achieves.** The axes to watch:

- **The trajectory of the revenue acceleration.** Growth went from **+37.8% (Q1 2026)** to **+220% (June)**. That rate will normalise; the question is to what — and whether the step-change in AI rack deployment sustains growth well above the company's historical pace.
- **Margin durability.** The **77.74% gross margin** is the entire investment case. Watch it for signs of customer cost-down pressure or second-sourcing, and treat any sustained decline as the most important signal this company can give.
- **Content per rack.** Whether heavier, liquid-cooled AI racks continue to require **higher-specification rail systems**, lifting revenue per unit rather than only unit volumes.
- **The 2025Q2 question and capital allocation.** Whether the unexplained one-off recurs, and what the company does with a **cash pile exceeding two-thirds of its balance sheet**.

Bottom line: King Slide is one of the purest examples in this collection of **where profit actually pools in a supply chain** — a maker of server rails earning a **77.7% gross margin, 67% operating margin and 34% return on equity**, nearly debt-free, with **~30% of the global market** and revenue growing **more than 200% year-on-year** as AI racks proliferate. It is also a **single-product company priced at ~25× book** with **one quarter in its recent record that nobody has publicly explained**. Judge it on **gross-margin durability and the normalised growth rate** — an exceptional niche monopoly, bought at a price that requires it to stay one.
